[[File:Leonhard Euler.jpg|thumb|upright|By 1772, [[Leonhard Euler]] had proven that 2,147,483,647 is a [[prime number|prime]].]]

The [[number]] '''2147483647'''{{efn|Pronounced two billion one hundred forty-seven million four hundred eighty-three thousand six hundred forty-seven.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Vanovschi |first=Vitalii |title=Properties of the number 2147483647 |url=http://www.numberempire.com:80/2147483647 |access-date=2026-09-01 |website=www.numberempire.com |language=en}}</ref>}} is the eighth [[Mersenne prime]], equal to 2<sup>31</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1. It is one of only four known [[double Mersenne number|double Mersenne primes]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/DoubleMersenneNumber.html |title=Double Mersenne Number |work=MathWorld |publisher=Wolfram Research |access-date=29 January 2018}}</ref>

The [[Primality test|primality]] of this number was proven by [[Leonhard Euler]], who reported the proof in a letter to [[Daniel Bernoulli]] written in 1772.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dunham |first=William |url=https://archive.org/details/eulermasterofusa0000dunh |title=Euler: the master of us all |publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]] |year=1999 |isbn=978-0-88385-328-3 |series=The Dolciani mathematical expositions |location=Washington, D.C. |page=[https://archive.org/details/eulermasterofusa0000dunh/page/4 4] |url-access=registration}}</ref> Euler used [[trial division]], improving on [[Pietro Cataldi]]'s method, so that at most 372 divisions were needed.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gautschi |first=Walter |title=Mathematics of computation, 1943-1993: a half-century of computational mathematics; Mathematics of Computation 50th Anniversary Symposium, August 9-13, 1993, Vancouver, British Columbia |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |year=1994 |isbn=978-0-8218-0291-5 |editor-last=Gautschi |editor-first=Walter |series=Proceedings of symposia in applied mathematics |volume=48 |location=Providence, RI |page=486}}</ref> It thus improved upon the previous record-holding prime, 6,700,417 – also discovered by Euler – forty years earlier. The number 2,147,483,647 remained the [[largest known prime]] until 1867.<ref name="The Largest Known Prime by Year">{{cite web |last=Caldwell |first=Chris |date=8 December 2009 |url=https://primes.utm.edu/notes/by_year.html |title=The Largest Known Prime by Year: A Brief History |website=The Prime Pages |publisher=University of Tennessee at Martin |access-date=29 January 2018}}</ref>

In computing, this number is the largest value that a [[Signed number|signed]] [[32-bit]] integer field can hold.

==Barlow's prediction==
At the time of its discovery, 2,147,483,647 was the [[largest known prime number]]. In 1811, [[Peter Barlow (mathematician)|Peter Barlow]] wrote (in ''An Elementary Investigation of the Theory of Numbers''):

<blockquote>Euler ascertained that 2<sup>31</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1 = 2147483647 is a prime number; and this is the greatest at present known to be such, and, consequently, the last of the above [[perfect number]]s [i.e., 2<sup>30</sup>(2<sup>31</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1)], which depends upon this, is the greatest perfect number known at present, and probably the greatest that ever will be discovered; for as they are merely curious, without being useful, it is not likely that any person will attempt to find one beyond it.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Barlow |first=Peter |author-link=Peter Barlow (mathematician) |url=https://archive.org/details/anelementaryinv00barlgoog |title=An Elementary Investigation of the Theory of Numbers |publisher=J. Johnson & Co. |year=1811 |location=London |page=[https://archive.org/details/anelementaryinv00barlgoog/page/n65 43] |oclc=1191003275}}</ref></blockquote>

He repeated this prediction in his work from 1814, ''A New Mathematical and Philosophical Dictionary''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Barlow |first=Peter |author-link=Peter Barlow (mathematician) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Y-csAAAAYAAJ&q=2147483647&pg=PT544 |title=A New Mathematical and Philosophical Dictionary: Comprising an Explanation of Terms and Principles of Pure and Mixed Mathematics, and Such Branches of Natural Philosophy as Are Susceptible of Mathematical Investigation |publisher=G. and S. Robinson |year=1814 |location=London |oclc=889473251}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Shanks |first=Daniel |title=Solved and Unsolved Problems in Number Theory |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-8218-2824-3 |edition=4th |location=Providence, Rhode Island |page=495}}</ref> In 1867, the number 3,203,431,780,337 was proven to be prime.<ref name="The Largest Known Prime by Year"/>

==In computing==
The number 2,147,483,647 (or [[hexadecimal]] 7FFFFFFF<sub>16</sub>) is the maximum positive value for a [[32-bit]] signed [[Integer (computer science)|binary integer]] in [[computing]]. It is therefore the maximum value for variables declared as integers (e.g., as <code>int</code>) in many programming languages.

The data type [[time_t]], used on operating systems such as [[Unix]], is a signed integer counting the number of seconds since the start of the [[Unix epoch]] ([[midnight]] [[UTC]] of 1 January 1970), and is often implemented as a 32-bit integer.<ref>{{Cite web |year=2004 |title=The Open Group Base Specifications Issue 6 IEEE Std 1003.1, 2004 Edition (definition of epoch) |url=http://www.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/000095399/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081219153936/http://www.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/000095399/ |archive-date=19 December 2008 |access-date=7 March 2008 |website=[[IEEE]] and [[The Open Group]] |publisher=[[The Open Group]]}}</ref> The latest time that can be represented in this form is 03:14:07&nbsp;UTC on Tuesday, 19&nbsp;January&nbsp;2038 (corresponding to 2,147,483,647 seconds since the start of the epoch). This means that systems using a 32-bit <code>time_t</code> type are susceptible to the [[Year 2038 problem]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.2038bug.com/ |title=The Year-2038 Bug |access-date=9 April 2009 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090318084855/http://www.2038bug.com/| archive-date= 18 March 2009 <!--DASHBot-->| url-status= live}}</ref>

On 1 January 2022, a bug was reported for [[Microsoft Exchange Server|Microsoft Exchange]] systems where email delivery would fail. An internal malware scanner (enabled by default since 2013) used the date and time as a signed 32-bit integer. The integer would change during the new year to 2,201,010,001 (with the first two digits representing the year), surpassing the maximum value for this data type.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Abrams |first=Lawrence |date=January 1, 2022 |title=Microsoft Exchange year 2022 bug in FIP-FS breaks email delivery |url=https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/microsoft/microsoft-exchange-year-2022-bug-in-fip-fs-breaks-email-delivery/ |access-date=2 January 2022 |website=[[Bleeping Computer]]}}</ref>

=== In video games ===
The number 2,147,483,647 often becomes a hard limit for various statistics in video games, such as points or money, if they are represented by signed 32-bit integers (rather than [[Floating-point arithmetic|floating-point]], [[Double-precision floating-point format|double-precision]] or [[Arbitrary-precision arithmetic|arbitrary-precision]]).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Lever |first=Nik |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eV0My6PR9xIC&pg=PA149 |title=Director MX 2004 Games: Game Development with Director |date=2012-08-06 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-1-136-14525-4 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cockfield |first=Bryan |date=2018-09-19 |title=Final Fantasy Exploit Teaches 32-bit Integer Math |url=https://hackaday.com/2018/09/19/final-fantasy-exploit-teaches-32-bit-integer-math/ |access-date=2022-09-25 |website=Hackaday}}</ref> Going over this limit by legitimate means, or by modding or hacking the game, results in many different outcomes caused by [[integer overflow]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Byrne |first=Michael |date=12 April 2015 |title=32-Bit Integers and Why Old Computers Matter |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/32-bit-integers-and-why-old-computers-matter/ |access-date=2022-09-25 |website=[[Vice (magazine)|Vice]]}}</ref> The most common outcome is the number "wrapping" into the negatives. Another potential outcome is ''game crashing'', thus meaning there was no failsafe implemented in the event the value exceeds the signed 32-bit limit—generally if the underlying engine has undefined behavior, instead of a wraparound behavior, for integer overflow. A well-known example in video games is that of ''[[Old School RuneScape]] and [[Grand Theft Auto V]],'' where the number is used as the maximum amount of coins (or any other item) that a player can hold at once with normal methods, known as a "max cash stack".<ref>{{Cite web |date= |title=Coins |url=https://runescape.wiki/w/Coins|website=Runescape Official Wiki}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Wood |first=Austin |date=2018-07-12 |title=Old School Runescape pulled offline as billions of gold appear out of nowhere |language=en |work=PC Gamer |url=https://www.pcgamer.com/old-school-runescape-pulled-offline-as-billions-of-gold-appear-out-of-nowhere/ |access-date=2022-09-25 |quote=it's appropriate to check that the calculation doesn't overflow the max integer limit of the game's language (2.1 billion). Unfortunately, the logic used for this calculation was incorrect, and when executed on stacks of other items (not the pouch itself) the result was to convert the stack to 2.1b coins.}}</ref> In similar cases, where an [[Unsigned int|unsigned]] instead of signed 32-bit integer is used, the limit might be extended to [[4,294,967,295]].<ref name=":0" />
